access: PRIVATE: exclude until independent solutions are frozen.

models.model: fōt: fōt, fōtes, fēt, fōt, fēt, fōta, fōtum, fēt
models.target: Complete newly assigned root-noun paradigm; do not infer every oblique from the nominative.
models.explanation: Fōt has the inherited vowel alternation in its selected dative singular and nominative/accusative plural; genitive and dative plural retain fōt-. Do not apply one vowel throughout every cell.
models.alternatives: Accept only documented variants within their stated lexical and morphological cells.
models.diagnosis: Fōt has the inherited vowel alternation in its selected dative singular and nominative/accusative plural; genitive and dative plural retain fōt-. Do not apply one vowel throughout every cell.

models.model: brycg: brycg, brycge, brycge, brycge, brycga, brycga, brycgum, brycga; hęre: hęre, hęres, hęre, hęre, hęras, hęra, hęrum, hęras
models.target: Complete selected feminine brycg and masculine hęre systems, including their characteristic stem behavior.
models.explanation: Give all four cases in both numbers. Keep brycg’s checked stem and hęre’s independently specified oblique and plural forms; a familiar ending does not establish an unattested stem.
models.alternatives: Accept only documented variants within their stated lexical and morphological cells.
models.diagnosis: Give all four cases in both numbers. Keep brycg’s checked stem and hęre’s independently specified oblique and plural forms; a familiar ending does not establish an unattested stem.

models.explanation: Each complete indicative system has six present and six preterite positions. Distinguish contracted strong flēon from weak grētan and preserve the independently checked stems.
models.alternatives: Accept only documented variants within their stated lexical and morphological cells.
models.diagnosis: Each complete indicative system has six present and six preterite positions. Distinguish contracted strong flēon from weak grētan and preserve the independently checked stems.

models.explanation: The four requested positions expose present stem alternation, the strong second-singular/plural preterite stem, and the respective weak preterite formations. Select cells by person, number and tense before writing them.

models.target: Complete selected command pairs; keep imperative and indicative morphology distinct.
models.explanation: A singular command addresses one person; its plural counterpart addresses several. Use each verb’s checked command stem, without adding an indicative third-singular ending.
models.alternatives: Accept only documented variants within their stated lexical and morphological cells.
models.diagnosis: A singular command addresses one person; its plural counterpart addresses several. Use each verb’s checked command stem, without adding an indicative third-singular ending.

models.model: Ic hæbbe ðæt hūs geworht. Ic hæfde ðæt hūs geworht. Ðū hæfst ðæt hūs geworht. Ðū hæfdest ðæt hūs geworht. Hē hæfð ðæt hūs geworht. Hē hæfde ðæt hūs geworht. Wē habbað ðæt hūs geworht. Wē hæfdon ðæt hūs geworht. Gē habbað ðæt hūs geworht. Gē hæfdon ðæt hūs geworht. Hīe habbað ðæt hūs geworht. Hīe hæfdon ðæt hūs geworht.

construction_groups.label: Habban + object + past participle: present and preterite indicative

models.target: Complete twelve-position indicative compound pattern built from actual auxiliary forms, accusative object and selected participle; this is not a new set of synthetic endings or a claim to exhaust all moods.
models.explanation: The auxiliary is finite and changes for person, number and tense. The accusative object ðæt hūs and uninflected participle geworht stay fixed. These are twelve indicative construction positions, not twelve additional inflectional forms.
models.alternatives: The target requires the stated indicative positions and fixed object/participle. Other grammatical clauses or moods do not complete that requested table.
models.diagnosis: Do not inflect the participle for person or number, replace the accusative object with a passive subject, or confuse a preterite auxiliary with a present auxiliary.

models.model: gierwan: gierwende, gierwed; settan: sęttende, sętt; gewyrcean: gewyrcende, geworht
models.target: Complete two-member base systems and their explicit auxiliary use; no unassigned participial adjective endings.
models.explanation: These are present- and past-participle bases, not finite personal forms. Each retains its separately checked lexical stem; these six bases do not by themselves license an unassigned adjective declension.
models.alternatives: Accept only documented variants within their stated lexical and morphological cells.
models.diagnosis: These are present- and past-participle bases, not finite personal forms. Each retains its separately checked lexical stem; these six bases do not by themselves license an unassigned adjective declension.

models.model: The man came, and he saw the house. Arrival precedes seeing. Cōm and geseah are third-person singular preterite indicatives.
models.explanation: The coordinated narrative presents two successive completed events.
models.alternatives: An equivalent ordinary past English narration is valid.
models.diagnoses: Do not make the second verb an infinitive or replace narrative succession with an unsupported cause.
models.target: Simple preterites in ordinary successive narration.

models.model: The man saw the house which his son had built. Geseah and geworhte are morphologically preterite; the context places the building before the seeing.
models.explanation: English had built makes explicit a relation which the Old English expresses with a simple preterite in context. The relative ðe is the object of geworhte; his sunu is its subject.
models.alternatives: Which his son built is also grammatically possible English if the supplied order remains clear.
models.diagnoses: Do not call geworhte a morphological pluperfect or claim that the son built the house after the visit.
models.target: A simple Old English preterite can express an earlier past event when context supplies the relation.

models.model: I have built the house. / I had built the house. Ic names the builder; ðæt hūs is the accusative object; hæbbe/hæfde is finite; geworht is the past participle.
models.explanation: The present construction presents the completed action from the present viewpoint. The past construction presents it as prior to a past viewpoint. The same participle remains nonfinite.
models.alternatives: Natural contextual translations that preserve the stated relation are valid; word order may vary.
models.diagnoses: The house is not the grammatical subject of either sentence. Do not make geworht a second finite verb or turn the active construction into an agentless passive.
models.target: Present and past habban with a transitive past participle; active relation retained.

models.model: I have the house. / I have built the house. In the first, habban expresses possession; in the second it combines with geworht to present the subject’s completed building.
models.explanation: The object remains accusative in both. The participle adds an action and its completed/result relation; possession alone does not say that the possessor built it.
models.alternatives: A resultative paraphrase is defensible if it retains the subject’s relation to the building and acknowledges the instructed construction.
models.diagnoses: Do not infer building from bare hæbbe, or infer that the auxiliary itself carries the lexical meaning build.
models.target: Lexical possession versus the completed-action construction; a familiar finite surface does not establish the same function.

models.model: The man bound the horse. / The horse was bound. / The horse was bound. Mann is nominative subject of the active clause and hors its accusative object. In both passives hors is nominative subject. Only the first sentence names the binder.
models.explanation: Wearð often highlights the event of binding; wæs often presents the resulting state. Context can permit event readings with wesan, so the forms alone do not force two different English tenses.
models.alternatives: Was tied, became bound or stood bound may suit the relevant context. The neuter noun’s identical nominative/accusative shape does not erase its change of role.
models.diagnoses: Do not leave the active agent as the passive subject, invent a specified binder in the agentless clauses, or insist that wæs can never describe an event.
models.target: Active and passive participant structure; contextual limits of weorðan and wesan.

models.model: The man had departed / was gone. Wæs is finite preterite singular wesan; gewiten is the intransitive past participle of gewītan.
models.explanation: The man himself departs. The construction does not introduce an outside agent who departs him; it is an intransitive completed-action/result expression.
models.alternatives: Was gone suits the resultant state; had departed makes anteriority explicit in a past narrative.
models.diagnoses: Do not translate was departed as though departed were a transitive passive, or require an unnamed agent.
models.target: Wesan with intransitive past participle can express departure/anteriority; it is not mechanically passive.

models.model: The man sat / was sitting. Wæs is finite preterite singular wesan; sittende is a present participle.
models.explanation: A progressive rendering can fit an ongoing sitting context, but the Old English periphrasis does not mechanically impose the full modern English progressive system.
models.alternatives: An appropriate simple past or progressive is valid when its context is stated.
models.diagnoses: Do not analyse sittende as a finite present or a past participle, and do not infer present time from its name present participle.
models.target: Bounded recognition of wesan plus present participle; no universal modern progressive tense.

models.model: He says that he is here. / He said that he was here. Sægð is present indicative; sægde is preterite indicative. Sīe and wǣre are the respectively present and preterite subjunctive forms used in these reports.
models.explanation: The task fixes the presence as simultaneous with the saying. The past report’s wǣre refers to that past report-time, not necessarily to an earlier event. Subjunctive marks the reporting presentation, not the report’s falsity.
models.alternatives: Equivalent indirect English reports are valid. Context can license indicative reports in other tasks, but these sentences have the listed subjunctive forms.
models.diagnoses: Do not translate wǣre as necessarily had been, or treat the subjunctive as evidence that he was absent.
models.target: Present and past reports with simultaneous content and contextual subjunctive.

models.model: He said that he had built the house. Sægde is the main preterite; dependent hæfde is the finite preterite subjunctive in the selected report; geworht is the past participle; ðæt hūs is the accusative object.
models.explanation: The completed building is earlier than the saying. Hæfde has the same spelling as its indicative counterpart, so the reporting context and assigned interpretation matter.
models.alternatives: A grammatical alternative order such as hæfde ðæt hūs geworht preserves the analysis.
models.diagnoses: Do not claim that the spelling hæfde by itself uniquely identifies mood or that the house built the speaker.
models.target: Anterior reported content with past habban and a past participle; syncretic hæfde is analysed in its reporting context.

models.model: He said that he intended/wished to come. The coming is the intended action, viewed prospectively from the past saying.
models.explanation: Wolde with cuman reports intention; it does not by itself assert an actual arrival.
models.alternatives: Wanted to come is valid. Would come can convey the intention in context, but a purely automatic future translation loses the requested distinction.
models.diagnoses: Do not claim that he came, or call cuman a finite future tense.
models.target: Past willan in a report of intention; no automatic completed event or purely grammatical future.

models.model: He will come. / He wishes/intends to come. In the first, cymð is present indicative with future reference supplied by the expected-visit context. The second has volitional wille with the infinitive cuman.
models.explanation: The language does not require willan whenever English uses will. Conversely, willan can contribute an actual desire or intention.
models.alternatives: Is coming is acceptable English for the expected arrival; wants to come is acceptable for the second.
models.diagnoses: Do not add a new Old English future auxiliary to the first or erase the intended volitional meaning of the second.
models.target: Contextual future reference of present indicative contrasted with lexical volition.

models.model: Wē habbað ðæt hūs geworht.
models.explanation: Habbað agrees with first-person plural wē. The accusative object and past participle do not change merely because the builder is plural.
models.alternatives: An equivalent order such as Wē ðæt hūs geworht habbað is defensible. Documented agreement variants require their own correct analysis.
models.diagnoses: Do not use singular hæbbe with wē or give the object nominative subject force.
models.target: Productive completed-action construction with first plural auxiliary.

models.model: Hīe hæfdon ðæt hūs geworht.
models.explanation: Hæfdon is the preterite plural auxiliary; the task puts the building before another past event.
models.alternatives: Other grammatical positions of the object and participle are accepted. A simple preterite may express anteriority elsewhere but does not meet this requested periphrastic target.
models.diagnoses: Do not use the present auxiliary or claim that a participle changes into a preterite finite form.
models.target: Productive anterior construction with third plural auxiliary.

models.model: Ðā męnn bundon ðæt hors. Ðæt hors wearð bunden.
models.explanation: The plural active subject gives bundon; the passive has singular hors as subject and therefore wearð. The passive leaves the binder unexpressed.
models.alternatives: A grammatical passive with wæs can be valid language but does not meet the explicit weorðan target.
models.diagnoses: Do not preserve the plural auxiliary from the active subject after making the singular horse the subject.
models.target: Active accusative object becomes nominative passive subject; change finite number with the new subject.

models.model: Se munuc sægð ðæt hē sīe hēr. Se munuc sægde ðæt hē wǣre hēr.
models.explanation: The monk’s reported presence is simultaneous with the respective present or past saying. Sīe/wǣre give the required report subjunctive.
models.alternatives: Other documented copular subjunctive forms and defensible order may be accepted. An indicative report can be grammatical but differs from the stated target.
models.diagnoses: Do not introduce an anterior had been relation or change the monk into another person.
old_english_outputs: Se munuc sægð ðæt hē sīe hēr.
Se munuc sægde ðæt hē wǣre hēr.
models.target: Reported sequence with explicit simultaneous relation, retained reference and appropriate finite forms.

models.model: Hē sægde ðæt hē ðæt hūs geworht hæfde.
models.explanation: Hæfde is selected as the reporting preterite subjunctive. The past auxiliary plus participle presents building anterior to the report.
models.alternatives: Hē sægde ðæt hē hæfde ðæt hūs geworht retains the same roles and relation.
models.diagnoses: Do not analyse both hæfde and geworht as finite verbs or substitute an agentless house-subject clause.
old_english_outputs: Hē sægde ðæt hē ðæt hūs geworht hæfde.
models.target: Earlier action within a past report, without mistaking the participle for a finite verb.

models.model: Hē sægde ðæt hē wolde cuman.
models.explanation: The reported intention is prior to its prospective fulfillment; actual fulfillment is not asserted.
models.alternatives: A defensible alternate word order preserves the target; intended, wished or wanted are appropriate English meanings.
models.diagnoses: Do not replace the intention with an asserted simple preterite arrival.
old_english_outputs: Hē sægde ðæt hē wolde cuman.
models.target: Reported intention and its temporal relation, not a mechanical would-to-past rule.

models.model: Giere ðone męte. Ic hæbbe ðone męte gierwed.
models.explanation: Giere is the singular command; męte remains the accusative thing prepared. In the reply hæbbe is finite and gierwed the selected participle.
models.alternatives: Documented gierwan spellings/participle alternatives and grammatical object placement are valid.
models.diagnoses: Do not confuse singular giere with plural gierwað, or use the preterite finite gierede in the participle slot.
models.target: New accusative-object frame and past-participle construction built on the known command and indicative auxiliary.

models.model: Sēo brycg wæs geworht. Ðā cōm mann.
models.explanation: The completed bridge is the subject of the first clause; the newcomer is the subject of the second. Brycg is feminine. The requested indefinite a does not require cardinal ān.
models.alternatives: A defensible order or explicit subject phrasing is valid. In an appropriate context weorðan can form a valid passive, but the prompt requires wesan here.
models.diagnoses: Do not give brycg a neuter or masculine article, or call cōm a second participle.
models.target: Passive result followed by narrated event; correct feminine subject and independently inflected arrival verb.

models.model: The man had built one house. Then his son came, and the son saw the house. The father said, “Now I have built the house.” The son said that he intended to travel. When the son departed, the father sat in the house. Then the son came, and he gave his father food.
models.explanation: Keep the first completed building before the first arrival; direct ic belongs to the father, whereas the later report concerns the son. The son’s departure and return are separately narrated.
models.alternatives: Intended/wanted to go or travel are equivalent; sat/was sitting may suit the simple preterite’s context. One house preserves assigned cardinal ān.
models.diagnoses: Do not identify every hē with the father, change the son’s intention to an asserted event before the next clause, or lose the return with food.
models.target: Connected independent interpretation using productive records; no source-only help.

models.model: Building the house → the son’s first arrival → the father’s announcement → the son’s departure → the son’s return with food. Hæfde … geworht puts the building before the first arrival.
models.explanation: The account then narrates the announced intention and its subsequent departure separately.
models.alternatives: A prose description of the same sequence is equivalent.
models.diagnoses: Do not put the building after the announcement or treat the return as the first arrival.
models.target: Reconstruct connected sequence from finite tense, periphrasis and discourse.

models.model: Ic is the father in his own quoted speech. Hē after ðæt refers to the son whose intention is reported. Hē in the last sentence is the returning son, who gives his father food. Se sunu gewāt separately narrates the departure.
models.explanation: The reporting verb alone does not guarantee fulfillment; the following narrative supplies it.
models.alternatives: A carefully explained contextual reference is required, not a claim that masculine morphology uniquely identifies the father or son.
models.diagnoses: Do not use the father as the giver to himself or infer completed travel solely from wolde.
models.target: Track reference and distinguish a reported intention from separately narrated fulfillment.

models.model: Ic is the subject and ðæt hūs the accusative object. Ðæt hūs is geworht.
models.explanation: The passive/result sentence makes the house nominative subject and leaves its builder unexpressed.
models.alternatives: A suitable order such as Geworht is ðæt hūs is valid. Present is meets the requested wesan target.
models.diagnoses: Do not retain ic as an agentless passive subject or claim that syncretic ðæt hūs has not changed syntactic role.
models.target: Apply active/passive argument distinction to an understood connected context.

models.model:
Then two peoples, the Picts from the north and the Scots from the west, began to attack them, take their possessions and plunder; and they oppressed and humbled them for many years. Then, in that unrest, they sent messengers to Rome with letters and a weeping petition. They asked them for help and promised them humble obedience and constant submission if they helped them so that they might overcome their enemies. Then they sent them a large army for support; and as soon as they came onto this island they fought against their enemies, inflicted great slaughter on them, and drove and expelled them from their borders. They instructed them to build a fortification for their protection against their enemies; and so they went home with great victory.

When the former adversaries then perceived this, that the Roman army had gone away, they soon came with a fleet onto their frontiers, struck down and killed all whom they encountered, trampled them like ripe crops and destroyed them, and utterly oppressed them.
models.explanation: The first subject is the raiding Picts/Scots; the petitioners are Britons; the sending and relieving army are Roman; the final attackers are the former adversaries. Preserve the complete raid–appeal–relief–withdrawal–renewed-raid chain and the final figurative destruction.
models.alternatives: A natural full translation may use closely related words for oppression, submission, support, borders and fortification. It must preserve who acts on whom and the prior Roman departure.
models.diagnoses: Do not make the Britons send a Roman army to themselves, retain the Romans as the final raiders, translate intransitive gewiten as passive, or treat the crop comparison as a new literal field episode.
models.target: Connected source translation without demanding recall of supplied vocabulary or constructions.

models.model: First raids → appeal to Rome → Roman relief → Roman withdrawal → renewed attack. The former adversaries discover that the Roman army has gone away, and then return.
models.explanation: The departure precedes their discovery; their renewed attack follows it in the narrative.
models.alternatives: Equivalent wording or a correctly labeled timeline is valid.
models.diagnoses: Do not reverse discovery and withdrawal or omit the first successful relief.
models.target: Reconstruct the full historical sequence and the attackers’ discovery.

models.model: The first Ðā introduces when; the second ðā is the correlating/temporal then within the clause; the third ðā is the nominative plural article with ǣrran gewinnan. The first ðæt is anticipatory that/this, object of ongēaton, explained by the following ðæt content clause.
models.explanation: The original note distinguishes when, then and the. Shared spelling does not establish identical grammatical work.
models.alternatives: A careful explanatory translation such as When the former enemies then realised this, that … is valid.
models.diagnoses: Do not make all three ðā articles, call the anticipatory object a relative pronoun, or confuse it with the subsequent content conjunction.
models.target: Exact source temporal correlation, article and anticipatory object; supplied higher structure stays supported.

models.model: The Britons send the messengers to Rome; the Romans send the army to the Britons; the Roman soldiers fight the enemies.
models.explanation: These are contextual referents of plural hīe. The original notes explicitly identify the legionaries and the Britons’ borders; morphology alone does not name a people.
models.alternatives: The Roman authority may be described generally as the Romans rather than naming a particular emperor not identified in the passage.
models.diagnoses: Do not assume that repeated hīe must retain one subject throughout or import a named ruler absent from the assigned span.
models.target: Subject reference across repeated plural pronouns; context and source apparatus, not morphology alone.

models.model: Wæs is third-singular preterite wesan, agreeing with se Rōmanisca hęre; onweg means away; gewiten is the past participle of intransitive gewītan. The Roman departure precedes the enemies’ perception of it.
models.explanation: The army itself has departed; it is not an object that an unnamed agent has departed.
models.alternatives: Had gone away or was gone expresses the context.
models.diagnoses: Do not treat the phrase as a transitive passive or place the withdrawal after the enemies return.
models.target: Intransitive departure periphrasis and past anteriority in exact source context.

models.model: Hīe (the Romans) is subject; him (the Britons) is the dative recipient; micelne hęre is the accusative object. An English passive is: Then a large army was sent to them for support.
models.explanation: Cook’s note compares an active Old English clause with passive Latin. The English passive changes the syntactic subject while preserving the affected army and recipient.
models.alternatives: A large army was then sent to the Britons to help them is equivalent. Latin analysis is not required.
models.diagnoses: Do not make the Britons the army being sent, or claim that Old English onsęndon is itself passive.
models.target: Voice comparison from actual participant structure, using the supplied source note.

models.model: They recommend that the Britons build a fortification for their protection. The building is prospective from the instruction, and the clause itself does not say that the building was completed.
models.explanation: The source’s dependent worhten belongs to the past reporting setting; morphological past does not make the recommended action anterior to the advice.
models.alternatives: Instructed/advised them to build a fortification conveys the relationship.
models.diagnoses: Do not translate they had already built merely from the past-shaped dependent verb, or add an unexpressed completed construction event.
models.target: Reported instruction and relative time, with source-only instruction frame supplied.

models.model: The victims are the people encountered by the returning attackers, the Britons in this narrative. The comparison pictures them being trampled and destroyed as ripe crops might be.
models.explanation: It intensifies the account of human devastation; the local gloss supplies the particular crop sense of ierðe.
models.alternatives: Ripe crop, ripe corn or a ripe field can work if the figurative reference is clear and the full violent action remains.
models.diagnoses: Do not introduce an unrelated literal harvest or make the Romans the final victims merely because they were the preceding army.
models.target: Literal form, figurative comparison and contextual referent within the connected reading.

models.model: Æt nīehstan se cyning geswāc rīces.
models.target: Bounded at-length expression; preterite cease with genitive rule/domain, rather than a manufactured infinitival bear-rule construction.

models.model: Hē hæfde ðæt rīce fēowertig gēara.
models.target: Possessed kingdom and forty-year duration; distinguish lexical had from a perfect auxiliary and retain the numeral scaffold.

models.model: Hwonne wurdon ðā brycga geworht?
models.target: Direct when question, plural bridge subject and past agentless passive with the newly assigned building participle.

models.model: Tō-dæg ðū bist mid mē.
models.target: Today and future-state context with the taught copular series; accompanying person in the dative.

models.model: Hwæt geworhton Rōmane on Breotone?
models.target: Accusative what question, Roman plural subject and explicitly requested preterite build; bounded Britain location.

models.model: Ic sęnde mīnne ęngel beforan ðīnum andwlitan.
models.target: Present send with accusative sent person, agreeing possessives and the specified before phrase; preserve the original face wording.

models.model: Cum, and bring ðā gewritu ðe ðū write.
models.target: Singular coming/bringing commands, plural letter object and relative object clause with a stated selected you-number; preserve the original ambiguous unnumbered you.

models.model: Ic gehāte ēow gehīersumnesse, gif gē mē helpen.
models.target: Promised thing and dative promisee; the source196d control calls for the selected dependent subjunctive in the if clause.

models.model: Sęnd mē micelne hęre.
models.target: Command send with dative recipient and masculine accusative army, with adjective agreement and no translated indefinite article.

models.model: Ic feohte wið mīne fīend.
models.target: First-person present fighting with the opponent governed by the selected with construction; possessive agrees with plural enemies.

models.model: Ādrīfað ēowre fīend.
models.target: Expulsion command and accusative foes; selected singular/plural addressee must match the possessive.

models.model: Ðā cęmpan fōron hām.
models.target: Plural soldier subject, simple preterite travel and directional home.

models.model: Hē cymð mid sciphęre.
models.target: Future reference without a compulsory willan auxiliary; accompanying collective fleet and omitted indefinite article.

models.model: Sleah ealle ðā ðe ðū gemētst.
models.target: Explicit singular command and all-who relative object; the finding verb has its own selected finite form.

models.model: Se hærfest is welig on wæstmum.
models.target: Singular harvest, rich predicate and the separately scoped in-fruits relation.

models.model: Sǣdtīma and hærfest ne geswīcað nǣfre.
models.target: Coordinated seedtime/harvest subjects, intransitive cease/fail and bounded never/future reference; do not infer the complete negative-concord system.

models.model: Ðæt gēar hæfð fēower tīda.
models.target: Lexical possession, four and the selected season sense; ordinary have is distinguished from the auxiliary construction.

models.model: Sēo eorðe is dryhtnes.
models.target: Predicate possession by a genitive title; obey Cook’s article omission.

models.model: Se sǣ geseah, and hē flēah.
models.target: Personified sea as seeing and fleeing subject; the selected masculine lexical gender governs pronoun reference.

models.model: Hē flīehð ðæt īserne wǣpen.
models.target: Future-reference flee with accusative thing avoided and full agreement of the iron adjective.
